sections.h: The food of angels (Wisdom of Solomon 16)
sections.b: The Wisdom of Solomon, in the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testament, gives the fullest early Jewish praise of the manna. Following the Greek Psalm 77:25 it calls the manna "the food of angels" (the Hebrew of Psalm 78:25 says "bread of the mighty ones"). It says the manna was "in tune with every taste" and "changed into whatever each one wished" (Wisdom of Solomon 16:20–21), a tradition the Talmud also keeps (Yoma 75a). It stood up to fire yet melted in the sun, so that people would learn to thank God before sunrise (16:22–28), and it taught that God's word, not crops, keeps people alive (16:26; Deuteronomy 8:3). In 19:21 it even calls the manna "ambrosial food," the Greek word for the food of the gods. Catholic worship sings 16:20 after the Tantum ergo at Benediction.
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 16:20–29; Wisdom of Solomon 19:21; Psalm 78:24–25; Exodus 16:14–31; Numbers 11:7–9; Deuteronomy 8:3; John 6:31–35

common: The manna in Wisdom 16:20 is the source of the Benediction response "Having within it all sweetness."
uncommon: Some read Wisdom 16:21's hypostasis as God's own nature showing itself in the manna.

sections.h: Not the snake but the Savior (Wisdom of Solomon 16:5–14)
sections.b: Wisdom retells Numbers 21 and calls the bronze snake "a token of salvation" (σύμβολον) that reminded Israel of God's law. "The one who turned to it was not saved by the thing he looked at, but by you, the Savior of all" (Wisdom of Solomon 16:7). The Mishnah later asks the same question, "Did the serpent kill, or did the serpent preserve life?" and answers that healing came when Israel turned their hearts to their Father in heaven (Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 3:8). Both guard against the magic that led Hezekiah to destroy the snake (2 Kings 18:4). John 3:14–15 reads the lifted snake as a figure of the Son of Man.
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 16:5–14; Numbers 21:4–9; 2 Kings 18:4; John 3:14–15

sections.h: The plagues as paired contrasts (Wisdom of Solomon 11–19)
sections.b: The Wisdom of Solomon retells the plagues not in order but in seven pairs, each showing that "what a person sins with, he is punished with" (Wisdom of Solomon 11:16) and that what punished Egypt helped Israel: vermin and quail, deadly locusts and flies against healed snakebite, hail with fire against manna, darkness against the pillar of fire, the firstborn struck and spared, the sea that drowned and the sea crossed (16:1–19:9). It adds details Exodus does not have (deadly locusts, phantoms in the darkness, warning dreams) as interpretation, and it reads the plagues as creation turned against Egypt (19:10).

sections.h: The all-powerful word (Wisdom of Solomon 16 and 18)
sections.b: In Wisdom God's word heals ("your word, Lord, which heals all things," 16:12; compare Psalm 107:20), feeds ("your word keeps safe those who believe in you," 16:26; compare Deuteronomy 8:3) and judges: at midnight "your all-powerful word, a warrior without mercy, sprang down from the heavens" with a sharp sword to strike Egypt's firstborn (Wisdom of Solomon 18:15–16). Jewish readers take this as a vivid figure for God acting. Christians read it with John 1:1–14 and Revelation 19:13–15, and the Western church sings 18:14–15 at Christmas in the Introit Dum medium silentium.
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 16:12; Wisdom of Solomon 16:26; Wisdom of Solomon 18:14–16; Psalm 107:20; John 1:1–14; Revelation 19:13–15; Hebrews 4:12

sections.h: The Exodus as creation remade (Wisdom of Solomon 19)
sections.b: Wisdom ends with the crossing of the sea told as a new creation: "the whole creation, each part in its own kind, was shaped again from the start" (Wisdom of Solomon 19:6). Dry land rises from water, a green plain appears in the sea, and the elements are re-tuned like the strings of a harp (19:7, 18–21). Earlier, in Egypt, creation had run backward (gnats from the ground, frogs from the river, 19:10). Christians link the passage with Isaiah 43:16–19, 2 Corinthians 5:17 and Romans 8:21.
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 19:6–21; Genesis 1:9–25; Isaiah 43:16–19; 2 Corinthians 5:17; Romans 8:21; Revelation 21:1

sections.h: Sodom and Egypt compared (Wisdom of Solomon 19:13–17)
sections.b: The Wisdom of Solomon judges Sodom's sin as hostility to strangers, and Egypt's as worse: Sodom "refused to take in strangers they did not know," but Egypt "turned guests who had helped them into slaves" (Wisdom of Solomon 19:14). Egypt was also struck with blindness, like the men at Lot's door (19:17; Genesis 19:11, where the Greek uses the same rare word). Wisdom 10:6 calls Lot "a righteous man," as 2 Peter 2:7 does. Compare Ezekiel 16:49 (pride and neglect of the poor) and Jude 1:7 (sexual immorality).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 19:13–17; Wisdom of Solomon 10:6; Genesis 19:1–11; Ezekiel 16:49; Jude 1:7; 2 Peter 2:7

sections.b: Wisdom coins the word μισοξενία, "hatred of strangers" (found nowhere else in the Greek Old Testament), for Egypt's treatment of Jacob's family: welcomed "with feasting," then "crushed with cruel labor" (Wisdom of Solomon 19:13–16). It turns back on Egypt a charge that critics in Alexandria made against Jews; Josephus answers one of them, Apion, who said Jews swore to bear no goodwill to any foreigner (Against Apion 2.121).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 19:13–16; Genesis 47:5–6; Exodus 1:8–14; Exodus 22:21; Hebrews 13:2

sections.h: The blameless man with the censer (Wisdom of Solomon 18:20–25)
sections.b: Without naming him, Wisdom retells Aaron's act from Numbers 16:41–50. "A blameless man rushed to fight in their defense" (Wisdom of Solomon 18:21), with "the weapon of his own priestly service: prayer, and incense to make atonement" (Wisdom of Solomon 18:21). He stood between the living and the dead, won "with a word" by reminding God of the oaths to the fathers (Numbers records no words), and the destroyer gave way before his robe, which carried "the whole world" (18:22–25).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 18:20–25; Numbers 16:41–50; Exodus 32:13; Hebrews 7:25

sections.h: The high priest's robe as the world (Wisdom of Solomon 18:24)
sections.b: "For the whole world was on his ankle-length robe" (Wisdom of Solomon 18:24). Wisdom shares a Jewish tradition that the high priest's dress pictured the universe. Philo calls the robe "a copy and representation of the world" and says the world enters with the high priest when he prays (Life of Moses 2.117, 133); Josephus explains its parts as earth, sky, sun, moon and the zodiac (Antiquities 3.179–187). The "four rows of stones" are the breastpiece of Exodus 28:17–21, and the crown is the gold plate "Holy to the LORD" (Exodus 28:36).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 18:24; Exodus 28:4; Exodus 28:17–21; Exodus 28:36–38; Sirach 45:8–12

sections.b: "Gripped by its conscience, it always imagines the worst" (Wisdom of Solomon 17:11). In Swete's Greek Old Testament the noun συνείδησις appears only here and in Ecclesiastes 10:20 (where it means private thoughts), so Wisdom 17:11 is the first place in the Greek Bible where conscience accuses the guilty. The chapter goes on to call fear "reason's help betrayed" (17:12). Paul makes the word central (Romans 2:15).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 17:11–13; Ecclesiastes 10:20; Romans 2:15; 1 Corinthians 8:7

sections.b: Wisdom uses στοιχεῖα for the physical elements of the world (Wisdom of Solomon 7:17; 19:18). It explains the Exodus miracles as the elements changing roles "the way notes on a harp change what the melody is called and yet keep their own sound" (19:18): land animals in water, frogs on land, fire burning in water, fire sparing the ice-like manna (19:19–21). This is the physical sense of the word that Paul later uses in Galatians 4:3 and Colossians 2:8, and that 2 Peter 3:10 says will melt in fire.
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 7:17; Wisdom of Solomon 19:18–21; Galatians 4:3; Colossians 2:8; 2 Peter 3:10

sections.h: The night no fire could light (Wisdom of Solomon 17:1–18:4)
sections.b: Wisdom turns the three days of darkness (Exodus 10:21–23) into a chapter on guilt and fear. The Egyptians lie "prisoners of darkness," bound "with one chain of darkness," while "the whole world was bright with shining light" (Wisdom of Solomon 17:2, 18, 20). Their night is "a picture of the darkness that was going to take them in" (17:21), and their own guilt weighs more than the dark. Meanwhile God's "holy ones had the brightest light," the pillar of fire, and the law's "imperishable light" was to reach the world through them (18:1–4).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 17:1–18:4; Exodus 10:21–23; Exodus 13:21; Matthew 8:12; Jude 1:13; John 1:5

sections.h: The first Passover in Wisdom of Solomon 18
sections.b: Wisdom pictures the first Passover as a secret sacrifice in which the people "bound themselves to the divine law" to share blessings and dangers alike, while "the fathers were leading the songs of praise" (Wisdom of Solomon 18:9), as later Jews sang the Hallel at the Passover meal (Mishnah Pesachim 10:6). The night had been foretold to the fathers (18:6), and the death of the firstborn forced Egypt to confess Israel as "God's son" (18:13; Exodus 4:22). The Catholic Lectionary reads 18:6–9 on the Nineteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time, Year C.
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 18:5–13; Exodus 12:1–30; Exodus 12:42; Exodus 4:22–23

sections.h: The word as warrior (Wisdom of Solomon 18:15–16)
sections.b: Wisdom gives the warrior's role to God's word: "your all-powerful word, a warrior without mercy" comes down at midnight with "a sharp sword" and fills Egypt with death, "it reached to heaven, and yet it had set foot on the earth" (Wisdom of Solomon 18:15–16). Behind it stand "The LORD is a man of war" (Exodus 15:3), the destroyer of Exodus 12:23, and the angel with drawn sword "between earth and sky" (1 Chronicles 21:16). Revelation 19:13–15 gives the rider called "the Word of God" a sharp sword from his mouth. Earlier the book had armed God with creation itself (5:17–20).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 18:14–16; Wisdom of Solomon 5:17–20; Exodus 15:3; Exodus 12:23; 1 Chronicles 21:16; Revelation 19:13–15

sections.h: Prayer and incense as a weapon (Wisdom of Solomon 18:21)
sections.b: Wisdom calls Aaron's "prayer, and incense to make atonement" the weapon of his priestly service, by which he stood against God's fury and stopped the plague (Wisdom of Solomon 18:21; Numbers 16:46–48). It adds that he won "with a word," reminding God of the oaths and covenants made with the fathers (18:22), the same appeal Moses made in Exodus 32:13. Compare the incense and the prayers of the saints in Revelation 8:3–4.
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 18:21–23; Numbers 16:46–48; Exodus 32:13; Psalm 141:2; Revelation 8:3–4
